entities.name: Oxford University Press
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Oxford University Press (OUP), established in the 1480s when Oxford University acquired its first printing press, is the world's largest university press and one of the oldest publishing houses in continuous operation, producing the Oxford English Dictionary, Oxford World's Classics, and hundreds of millions of books, journals, and educational materials annually. As a department of the University of Oxford, all OUP's profits support the university's academic mission.

OUP's printing history begins in the 1480s with Oxford University's early engagement with Gutenberg's technology; the first book printed in Oxford appeared in 1478. The Press received its royal charter in 1586 under Elizabeth I — making it one of three 'privileged presses' (with Cambridge and the King's Printer) authorized to print the Bible. OUP's Bible Division has published over a billion Bibles, making it the world's largest Bible publisher.

The Oxford English Dictionary — begun in 1857, first completed in 1928, continuously updated since — is the greatest single work of English lexicography, documenting every English word's etymology and historical usage. J.R.R. Tolkien worked as an editor on the OED in the early 1920s before writing The Lord of the Rings. OUP's academic journals (over 400 journals), Oxford World's Classics, Oxford Handbooks, and educational publishing make it the most comprehensive scholarly publisher in English. Its annual revenue exceeds £900 million — remarkable for a department of a single university.
